intro:
**The Sarcastic Challenge of al-Naḍr**

The historical catalyst of al-Maʿārij is preserved in classical chronicles about al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, the cynical Qurayshi chieftain who stood before the Kaʿbah and offered the arrogant, sarcastic prayer recorded in Sūrah al-Anfāl (8:32 — *“And ˹remember˺ when they prayed, “O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or overcome us with a painful punishment.”*): *“O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment!”* Sūrah al-Maʿārij opens with an immediate, razor-sharp response to this challenge: *“A questioner asked about a punishment bound to happen (*sa'ala sā'ilun bi-ʿadhābin wāqiʿ*), to the disbelievers; of it there is no preventer, from Allah, Owner of the Ascending Stairways!”* (70:1–3). The sūrah warns the skeptic that his sarcastic wish for retribution will be granted with terrifying precision: on a Day when the sky becomes like molten brass, the mountains like carded wool, and no close friend will ask about his friend, though they are placed in full view of each other.

**The Structural Architecture and the Sanctuary of the Prayerful**

The architecture of Sūrah al-Maʿārij is organized across three distinct movements:

1. The Cosmic Dimension and the Unavailing Ransom (1–18): Opens with the inevitable punishment, commands the Prophet to maintain beautiful patience without complaint (*fa-ṣbir ṣabran jamīlā*), contrasting human short-sightedness (*“Indeed, they see it distant, but We see it near!”*, 70:6–7 — *“but We see it as inevitable”*). The divine voice thunders: *“By no means! Indeed, it is the Flame of Hell (*Ladhā*), stripping away the scalp, inviting him who turned his back and amassed wealth and hoarded it!”*

2. The Pathology of the Ego and the Eightfold Sanctuary (19–35): Delivers the profound psychological diagnosis of human anxiety: man is created *Halūʿ* (fretful, panicked in adversity, tight-fisted in prosperity). It immediately presents the exceptional community that escapes this neurosis: *“Except the prayerful (*illā al-muṣallīn*)”* (70:22). The movement seals their destiny: *“Those will be in gardens, honored.”*

3. The Deniers on the Horizon and the Race from the Graves (36–44): Rebukes the polytheists who rush toward the Prophet with craning necks, sitting on his right and left in mocking groups, asking sarcastically: *“Does every person among them aspire to enter a garden of pleasure? By no means! Indeed, We have created them from what they know!”* God swears a cosmic oath by the Lord of the Easts and the Wests that He is competent to replace them with a people better than them. The sūrah concludes by commanding the Prophet to leave them to converse and play until they meet their Day, portraying them emerging from their graves in haste as if racing toward an idol's shrine, eyes cast down, humiliation covering them: *“That is the Day which they were promised!”*

verses.1:
> A challenger has demanded a punishment bound to come

**Hastening Doom as Proof of Blindness**

Psychology explains why anyone would dare heaven to strike. The challenger treats God's delay as God's defeat, converting mercy into evidence against mercy. Scripture catalogs this disease across many passages: deniers bidding the Prophet to hasten torment (22:47 — *“They challenge you ˹O Prophet˺ to hasten the torment. And Allah will never fail in His promise. But a day with your Lord is indeed like a thousand years by your counting”*), demanding the Hour's date as though scheduling would domesticate it (10:50-51 — *“Tell them ˹O Prophet˺, “Imagine if His torment were to overcome you by night or day—do the wicked realize what they are ˹really˺ asking Him to hasten”*), treating the threat's postponement as its refutation (16:1 — *“The command of Allah is at hand, so do not hasten it. Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him in worship˺”*). Each instance shares one structure — impatience weaponized against patience. The Qur'anic reply never hurries; it warns that hurrying proves nothing except the hurrier's folly. Punishment delayed is not punishment denied but respite extended, and respite is the very mercy the mocker mistakes for weakness. This verse therefore diagnoses before it threatens. Behind the demand for doom stands a refusal to read time theologically, to see in each undisturbed morning a gift rather than an alibi. Blindness to mercy and blindness to wrath are one blindness.

**Mockery Disguised as a Question**

The sūrah opens mid-confrontation, with an unnamed figure demanding torment as though placing a wager. Arabic saʾala with the preposition bi- can mean either asking about something or calling for it, and the verse exploits that seam. Some exegetes read a question — someone asked the Prophet who would be punished and when — while most hear a taunt, a supplication hurled upward in contempt. The majority view fits the sūrah's arc better, since everything that follows answers swagger rather than curiosity. Tradition names the mocker: al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who is reported to have challenged God to rain stones from the sky if the message were true (8:32 — *“And ˹remember˺ when they prayed, “O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or overcome us with a painful punishment.”*), or by another report Abū Jahl himself. Both identifications agree on the essential point — this was no sincere inquiry. Sarcasm dressed as prayer reveals a heart that has mistaken divine patience for divine absence. The sūrah will spend its first breaths correcting that arithmetic.

**The Sūrah Continues Where al-Ḥāqqah Ended**

Placement illumines purpose. Al-Maʿārij belongs to the middle Makkan period and likely followed its predecessor closely, extending the Resurrection scenes of 69:18-37 — *“You will then be presented ˹before Him for judgment˺, and none of your secrets will stay hidden”* into fresh tableaux of terror and duty. Where the previous sūrah closed by vindicating the Book, this one opens by confronting those who mocked it — defense turning to counter-charge. Its very titles witness to the opening scene: Saʾala, "Someone Asked," preserves the challenger's verb, while al-Mawāqiʿ recalls the impending matters he summoned. The canonical title, al-Maʿārij, waits two verses ahead, naming the stairways of ascent that frame God's majesty. Such continuity rebukes any reading of sūrahs as loose anthologies. The challenger of verse 1 stands in the rubble of ʿĀd and Thamūd, inherits Pharaoh's drowned arrogance, and still dares to demand. The Book answers sustained defiance with sustained description, surrounding the mocker with witnesses.
verses.2:
> for the disbelievers—to be averted by none—

**The Punishment Has Named Owners**

Verse 1 announced a falling torment; verse 2 delivers its address label. "For the disbelievers" — lil-kāfirīna — assigns the demanded punishment to those who demanded it, closing the circle with judicial neatness. The definite article matters: not some hypothetical deniers but the disbelievers, the known party of mockers surrounding the Prophet. Exegetes keep the reference concrete, hearing the Quraysh scoffers who treated resurrection-talk as entertainment. Yet the label outgrows its first wearers, as Qur'anic categories always do, extending to everyone who replicates their stance toward warning. Grammar reinforces ownership through the lām of entitlement: this punishment belongs to them the way wages belong to earners. No transfer, no substitution, no clerical error will redirect it. The challenger asked for whom the torment was; the verse answers with a mirror. It was, all along, for him.

**The Day Lurks Behind the Words**

"Punishment" here points chiefly to the Last Day, though Badr supplied its down payment. The demand of verse 1 concerned the teaching about the Last Day — the Hour the Prophet preached — and verse 2 keeps that horizon fixed. Worldly calamities can sometimes be averted: walls hold, ransoms pay, storms pass. Only the final reckoning carries the absolute "none," because only there does every buffer dissolve. Exegetes therefore hear the Last-Day register beneath the historical occasion, reading Badr as installment and Resurrection as sum. The verse's brevity suits that vastness; a line this short can hold the Day only by refusing detail. Detail will come soon enough — skies like molten brass, mountains like wool, children offered as ransom. For now the sūrah contents itself with ownership and irreversibility, two nails enough to fasten attention. The next verse will then name the height from which this unstoppable sentence descends.
verses.3:
> from Allah, Lord of pathways of ˹heavenly˺ ascent

**The Punishment Comes From Allah Himself**

Verse 2 sealed every exit; verse 3 names the power that sealed them. "From Allah" — min Allāh — traces the falling torment to its uttermost origin, past angels, past causes, past all intermediaries. The preposition matters: punishment does not merely occur with God's permission but proceeds from His presence, bearing His signature. Such directness answers the challenger's dare precisely. He had invoked heaven as though heaven were empty; the verse replies that heaven's Lord heard, and the falling punishment carries His return address. Theology and terror merge here. Because the torment comes from Allah, no lesser power can intercept it — verse 2's "none" now gets its explanation. Idols cannot shield, patrons cannot ransom, and nature cannot absorb what the Almighty sends. The verse therefore completes a small ladder of dread: demanded in verse 1, assigned and sealed in verse 2, and now sourced in the One whom none can resist.
verses.4:
> ˹through which˺ the angels and the ˹holy˺ spirit will ascend to Him on a Day fifty thousand years in length

**Angels Climbing Toward Their Lord**

The verse opens heaven's traffic to view: angels ascending to Him along the pathways verse 3 named. The verb taʿruju pictures steady rising — ranks mounting through ranked skies toward the throne. Such scenes recur across the Book wherever majesty needs displaying: the night of decree fills with descending angels (97:4 — *“That night the angels and the ˹holy˺ spirit descend, by the permission of their Lord, for every ˹decreed˺ matter”*), while here the emphasis reverses into ascent on the Day of gathering. Direction carries doctrine. Upward movement means return to origin, completion of errands, delivery of records — creation's couriers coming home. The plural "angels" keeps their number vast and unnamed, an uncounted host streaming skyward. Against the lone challenger of verse 1, the verse arrays heaven's multitudes; against earth's flat horizons, it stacks height upon height. What the mocker demanded as spectacle has become spectacle beyond his imagining. Punishment will not crawl toward him across the sand. It will descend along roads crowded with ascending light.

**The Spirit Beside the Angels**

"The spirit" — al-rūḥ — stands distinguished from the angels though marching with them, and the distinction has exercised exegetes for centuries. Most identify the Spirit as Gabriel, the Trustworthy Spirit of Sūrah 26 (26:193 — *“which the trustworthy spirit ˹Gabriel˺ brought down”*), singled out by rank as a commander gets named apart from the troops. The singling honors rather than separates: Gabriel leads the ascent as he led revelation, first among bearers of divine business. Others propose a mighty angel distinct from Gabriel, or the collective spirits of the dead rising for judgment, or a created grandeur beyond angelic kind. Each minority view strains against the plain parallel with Sūrah 97, where the Spirit descends alongside angels in identical pairing. The strongest reading therefore keeps Gabriel, while admitting the verse's reserve — the Book names him by office here rather than by name, letting function outshine person. Whatever precision scholars debate, the scene's force survives: heaven's greatest, unnamed or named, climbs with heaven's many.

**Time Moves Differently Above the Sky**

The Book elsewhere confirms that heaven keeps its own clock. A day with your Lord measures like a thousand years of earthly counting (22:47 — *“They challenge you ˹O Prophet˺ to hasten the torment. And Allah will never fail in His promise. But a day with your Lord is indeed like a thousand years by your counting”*), and cosmic affairs ascend to Him through days of that millennial scale (32:5 — *“He conducts every affair from the heavens to the earth, then it all ascends to Him on a Day whose length is a thousand years by your counting”*). Such verses relativize every human timetable without dissolving accountability — the Day comes slowly by our impatience and suddenly by our readiness. The fifty thousand years here extend the same principle to its Last-Day extreme: the final Day dwarfs even the thousand-year days of providence. Physics offers no objection, since time was always a creature rather than a master; the Lord of ascents stretches and folds it at will.
verses.5:
> So endure ˹this denial, O Prophet,˺ with beautiful patience

**Patience Commanded at the Flashpoint**

Fa-ṣbir — "so endure" — lands immediately after the challenger's dare and heaven's four-verse reply. The sequence matters: first the Book answers the mocker with doom, then it steadies the Prophet with discipline. Argument without patience curdle into bitterness, so the sūrah prescribes composure at the exact moment provocation peaks. The fa- prefix draws the consequence tight: because punishment is certain and rescue impossible, the Prophet need not hurry, answer, or despair. Vindication travels on schedule; his task is stamina till it arrives. Such commands punctuate the Makkan years, where daily scorn made endurance the Prophet's primary warfare. Revelation managed his heart the way generals manage troops — with orders fitted to the battle's phase. Here the order is stillness. Let heaven's machinery grind; the Messenger's portion is beautiful patience.

**Beauty Qualifies the Endurance**

Ṣabran jamīlan — "beautiful patience" — refuses grim resignation. Jamīl means lovely, comely, gracious: patience worn the way fine garments are worn, without tearing. The phrase echoes Jacob's resolve when his sons brought Joseph's bloodied shirt — "beautiful patience!" he cried, twice over (12:18, 83 — *“So ˹I can only endure with˺ beautiful patience!”*). His model defines the term: no wailing to men, no complaint against heaven, grief carried upright before God alone. Exegetes therefore gloss beautiful patience as endurance without grievance aired to creatures, suffering that neither performs nor curdles. The adjective transforms a burden into an adornment. Anyone can wait; the Prophet must wait beautifully, his composure itself a sermon to watching Makkah. Strain will show — he was human — but strain need not sour. What the verse commands is not numbness but nobility under pressure.

**Patience Was Never Abrogated**

A famous dispute surrounds this verse. Some early commentators held that commands to endure unbelievers were later abrogated by permission to fight — patience as wartime tactic, superseded when swords were unsheathed. Others, led by al-Ṭabarī, insisted the command holds at all times and in all situations; still others classed it as definitive (muḥkam), unabrogatable by nature. The majority instinct favors permanence, and for principled reasons: abrogation touches specific legal rulings, not universal virtues (2:106 — *“If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything”*). Patience names a character, not a tactic — and characters do not expire with circumstances. And the Prophet practiced beautiful patience after power came, forgiving Makkah at its conquest when vengeance lay ready to hand. The stronger view therefore keeps the verse permanently open. Swords may answer armies, but only patience answers scorn.

Beyond its occasion, the verse founds a discipline. The sūrah will later list prayer's constancy among the righteous (70:22-23 — *“except those who pray consistently performing their prayers”*), and patience fuels that constancy — worship repeated across unrelieved years.
verses.6:
> They truly see this ˹Day˺ as impossible

**Distance Measured by Denial**

Baʿīdan — "far off" — diagnoses more than geography. The deniers deem the Day remote, and remoteness in their dialect means impossibility: what stands far enough away need never be faced. Exegetes gloss the term both ways — distant in time or impossible in fact — and the ambiguity is the point, since delay and denial feed each other. A threat postponed feels a threat dissolved; each quiet sunrise votes against the warnings. Such reasoning mistakes the map for the territory, treating personal unreadiness as cosmic unlikelihood. The verse exposes the maneuver with a single adjective. Farness here is not measured but manufactured — a moral verdict disguised as a calendar estimate. They call the Day far because nearness would demand repentance, and repentance is the one journey they refuse. Distance becomes disobedience spelled in miles.

**Scripture Repeats the Warning**

The Book returns to hastening-mockery across many chapters, building a dossier on delay-based doubt. One passage records deniers bidding the Prophet to hasten the punishment (22:47 — *“They challenge you ˹O Prophet˺ to hasten the torment. And Allah will never fail in His promise. But a day with your Lord is indeed like a thousand years by your counting”*); another warns that the Hour comes suddenly while they dispute (36:49-50 — *“They must be awaiting a single Blast, which will seize them while they are ˹entrenched˺ in ˹worldly˺ disputes Then they will not be able to make a ˹last˺ will, nor can they return to their own people”*); still others note the demand for instant doom as a standing symptom (16:1 — *“The command of Allah is at hand, so do not hasten it. Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him in worship˺”*; 29:53-54 — *“They challenge you ˹O Prophet˺ to hasten the punishment.”*). Each instance shares the structure verse 6 distills: distance assumed, urgency mocked, patience mistaken for impotence. Repetition across sūrahs signals typicality — this is not Makkah's quirk but humanity's reflex. Every age discounts futures it cannot invoice, treating postponement as permission. The Qur'an's persistence matches the disease's: warning restated till heeded or till arrival ends debate. Verse 6 condenses the whole file into one line. Behind its brevity stands a library of unheeded alarms, each now echoed in this single verdict of farness.
verses.7:
> but We see it as inevitable

**Two Verbs of Seeing Collide**

Yarawnahu against narāhu — "they see it" against "We see it" — the sūrah stages a collision of visions. Same verb, same object, opposite estimates: farness versus nearness, impossibility versus inevitability. The parallel grammar spotlights the only variable that matters — the seer. Deniers peer through cataracts of desire; God beholds through perfect knowledge. One sight guesses, the other knows. Such opposed pairing concentrates the whole passage's argument into two lines: verses 6-7 together form a scale, and every reader must choose which pan holds truth. The adversative "but" carries the verse's entire force, overturning human estimate with divine fact. No argument follows because none is needed — heaven's sight settles what earth's disputes. When God and mockers disagree about distance, only one of them has ever measured the road.

**Inevitable Comforts as It Threatens**

Qarīb cuts two ways, and the sūrah wields both edges. For deniers, nearness threatens — the doom they mocked approaches with quiet feet. For believers, nearness comforts — vindication they awaited stands at the door. Same Day, same nearness, opposite receptions: the difference lies completely in preparation. This duality explains the verse's placement after the command to beautiful patience (70:5 — *“So endure ˹this denial, O Prophet,˺ with beautiful patience”*). Patience needs a horizon, and "near" supplies it — endure beautifully, for relief approaches. Without nearness, patience sags into indefinite gloom; with it, endurance gains a finish line. The Prophet's hardest years so received their deepest consolation in one adjective. Every subsequent generation of the strained inherits the same syllable of hope. What threatens the scoffer steadies the sufferer, and the Book's economy wastes no word — one "near" serves two congregations.
verses.8:
> On that Day the sky will be like molten brass

**The Cosmos Begins to Melt**

Yawma takūnu — "on a Day when" — opens the gallery of horrors verse 7 promised. After estimates of distance, the sūrah displays the Day itself, beginning overhead. The sky, humanity's firmest ceiling, turns fluid first: solidity was always conditional, blueness a temporary lease. Cosmic unmaking follows a deliberate order across the Book's the teaching about the Last Day — heavens split, stars fall, mountains march, seas boil — and this passage contributes its own sequence from sky through mountains to abandoned friendships. Starting above the head maximizes dread; no shelter stands when shelter itself dissolves. The definite "that Day" points back to the punishment of verses 1-4 and the nearness of verse 7, binding description to warning. What deniers called far now gains a sky, a color, a texture. Vagueness was their refuge; detail evicts them.

**Hell's Drink Becomes Heaven's Roof**

A parallel passage sharpens the terror. Elsewhere the tree of punishment feeds sinners food like muhl, boiling in their bellies like scalding water (44:45 — *“Like molten metal, it will boil in the bellies”*). Same noun, same burning fluid — but there it is swallowed, while here it hangs overhead. The sūrah so merges two torments: hell's interior menu becomes the sky's exterior canopy. Above and within, the damned meet the same substance; no direction offers relief. Such cross-linking rewards readers who hold the Book whole — muhl in one chapter illuminates muhl in another, and the Day's sky gains its full horror only beside hell's cauldron. Craftsmanship of this kind weaves the teaching about the Last Day into a single fabric rather than scattered threats. The fluid damned souls will drink already glowers above unrepentant heads. Judgment's kitchen and judgment's ceiling stock the same brew.
verses.9:
> and the mountains like ˹tufts of˺ wool

**Mountains Soften to Wool**

Verse 8 melted the sky; verse 9 teases the mountains into fibers. Al-jibāl ka-l-ʿihn — mountains like carded wool — inverts the most fixed simile in human speech. Mountains mean permanence in every tongue; wool means lightness, drift, the handful that scatters at a breath. The Book stages this reversal identically in Sūrah 101 (101:5 — *“and the mountains will be like carded wool”*), where the same noun ʿihn describes the same unmaking. Doubled witness, single doom. ʿIhn means wool fluffed and teased for spinning — fibers separated, airy, adrift. What tectonics raised over eons, the Day unmakes in a moment. The conjunction "and" binds sky and peak into one collapse: above melts, beside dissolves, and between them no refuge stands. Geology itself will testify that only one permanence ever existed. When mountains go woolly, every lesser solidity has already failed.

**The Immovable Learns to Drift**

Proverbial firmness makes the mountains heaven's chosen exhibit. Humans swear by their stability — "firm as mountains" — and the Book elsewhere shows them passing like clouds on that Day (27:88 — *“Now you see the mountains, thinking they are firmly fixed, but they are travelling ˹just˺ like clouds.”*), reduced to shifting sand-heaps (73:14 — *“on the Day the earth and mountains will shake ˹violently˺, and mountains will be ˹reduced to˺ dunes of shifting sand”*), scattered to dust (77:10 — *“and the mountains are blown away”*). Each image attacks a different facet of trust: motion against fixity, sand against rock, dust against mass. Wool adds texture to the sequence — not merely moved but transformed, solidity unmade into softness. The progression teaches by accumulation: no single metaphor exhausts the unmaking, so metaphors multiply. What resists one image falls to the next. Readers who trust geography must watch every landmark dissolve in turn. The Day does not relocate the mountains; it redefines them. Immovable becomes ungraspable, and proverbs collapse with their referents.

**Carded, Dyed, Scattered**

ʿIhn repays lexical lingering. The noun evokes wool carded — teased apart by combs into separate strands — and some lexicographers add dyed in various colors, suggesting peaks loosened into drifting hues. Either way lightness dominates: fibers that winds toss, fingers part, and children scatter. Mountains will hang in the Day's air the way thistledown hangs in summer — visible, touchable, utterly without weight. The image also inverts creation's order, where mountains were set as pegs to steady the earth; pegs pulled, the tent collapses. Such reversal runs through the whole passage: skies melt, peaks drift, friendships freeze, children become currency.
verses.10:
> And no close friend will ask ˹about˺ their friends

**Friendship Freezes on That Day**

Lā yasʾalu ḥamīmun ḥamīman — no warm friend will ask after a warm friend. The doubled ḥamīm frames mutual intimacy: each was the other's confidant, table-companion, keeper of secrets. On that Day neither inquires. Asking after someone is friendship's smallest currency — a question costing nothing — yet even this copper goes unspent. Terror bankrupts affection completely. The verse's absoluteness startles: not "few will ask" but none, loves dissolved universally. Exegetes stress the contrast with tribal solidarity, where kinsmen ransomed kinsmen and friends vouched for friends; the Day voids every such bond. What melts skies and wools mountains also freezes hearts. Social warmth was always weather, and the Day changes the climate. No inquiry, no greeting, no glance of recognition spared — each soul audits itself alone.

**Terror Privatizes Every Soul**

The Book explains this solitude across several passages. On that Day each person's own affair will suffice and swallow them (80:37 — *“For then everyone will have enough concern of their own”*); no kinship will function between them, nor will they ask after one another (23:101 — *“Then, when the Trumpet will be blown, there will be no kinship between them on that Day, nor will they ˹even care to˺ ask about one another”*); no bearer will carry another's burden (35:18 — *“No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another.”*); parent and child will find the reckoning unshareable (31:33 — *“O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord, and beware of a Day when no parent will be of any benefit to their child, nor will a child be of any benefit to their parent.”*). Together these texts draw one portrait: dread so total it monopolizes attention. Drowning swimmers cannot save each other; the Day drowns every soul separately. Preoccupation is not cruelty but incapacity — hearts have no surplus left for courtesy. Such privatization reverses earthly life, where attention overflows toward others. The verse so measures terror by its social cost: whatever unmakes friendship has unmade everything smaller too. When ḥamīm ignores ḥamīm, no bond on earth has survived. Solitude is the Day's universal uniform.

**The Warm Friend Goes Cold**

Ḥ-m-m, the root of ḥamīm, means heat — boiling water, fevered brow, passionate concern. The close friend is literally the warm one, heated with loyalty. The verse chills that warmth absolutely: the hot go cold, the near go strange. Etymology sharpens the pathos — language itself testifies what the Day destroys. Intimacy's vocabulary survives while intimacy perishes; ḥamīm still means warm friend, but no warm friends remain to bear the name. The Book loves such hollowed words, letting familiar terms echo in emptied halls.
verses.11:
> ˹although˺ they will be made to see each other. The wicked will wish to ransom themselves from the punishment of that Day by their children

**They Will See and Still Abandon**

Yuṣṣarūnahum — "they will be made to see them" — grants vision while withholding mercy. Friends behold friends, kin recognize kin, yet verse 10's silence holds. Exegetes debate the tableau's arrangement: most hear mutual sight, all humanity exposed to all, recognition without rescue. Some report God displaying the damned to the believers as vindication; others hear angels shown the states of souls for witness. The majority reading carries the verse's main terror — seeing and abandoning together. Blindness would have been kinder; sight sharpens solitude into spectacle. Each soul watches beloved faces pass toward ruin, hands lowered, voice stilled. The passive verb assigns heaven's agency: God shows them to each other, staging recognition as part of reckoning. What eyes meet, hearts cannot help. Vision becomes a new faculty of torment.

**Ransom Refused in Advance**

Scripture pre-refuses every such offer. Were the wicked to have earth's full weight in gold and tender it entire, acceptance would still be denied (3:91 — *“Indeed, if each of those who disbelieve then die as disbelievers were to offer a ransom of enough gold to fill the whole world, it would never be accepted from them.”*); though they owned all the world and its double besides, ransom would fail (13:18 — *“As for those who do not respond to Him, even if they were to possess everything in the world twice over, they would certainly offer it to ransom themselves.”*); no soul's bargain avails, no intercession profits the unpermitted (10:54 — *“If every wrongdoer were to possess everything in the world, they would surely ransom themselves with it.”*; 2:48 — *“Guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another. No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given”*). The dossier is comprehensive — wealth refused, substitutes refused, mediation restricted. Justice on that Day runs non-negotiable: each soul answers for itself, tendering only its record. This foreclosure explains "will wish" — the verb of futile desire. Wishing replaces transacting because no market operates. The verse so tortures with impossibility: the wicked conceive the bid heaven has already voided. Hope of ransom becomes another torment, imagination drafting contracts the court shreds. Severity here is honesty — better to learn refusal now, while repentance still functions as currency, than to draft bids in fire.
verses.12:
> their spouses, their siblings

**The Ransom Widens to the Household**

Wa-ṣāḥibatihi wa-akhīh — "his spouse and his brother" — continues the auction verse 11 opened. Children failed as tender; now the wicked bid the household's remaining pillars. The verse's extreme brevity — three words in Arabic — quickens the bidding's rhythm, lots flashing past like auctioneer's patter. Each lot names a bond: spouse, the companion of bed and board; brother, the sharer of blood and name. Together they exhaust the intimate circle — offspring already offered, partner and sibling now added. The wicked strip their own lives bare lot by lot, tendering every love in turn. Escalation works by accumulation: each verse piles more beloveds onto the voided bid. Heaven's silence answers each lot identically. The auctioneer will not pause; the court will not accept. Only the lots grow, and the growing is the torment.

**What Ransom Cannot Buy**

Refusal stands pre-recorded across the Book. No ransom gets accepted from any soul, however tendered (2:48, 123 — *“Guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another. No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given”*); no earth-full of gold suffices (3:91 — *“Indeed, if each of those who disbelieve then die as disbelievers were to offer a ransom of enough gold to fill the whole world, it would never be accepted from them.”*); doubled worlds would fail alike (13:18 — *“As for those who do not respond to Him, even if they were to possess everything in the world twice over, they would certainly offer it to ransom themselves.”*); ransom-seeking on that Day finds no market (57:15 — *“So Today no ransom will be accepted from you ˹hypocrites˺, nor from the disbelievers.”*). The dossier's unanimity is the point — heaven's court takes no payment, period. Justice there is not for sale at any price because mercy already offered itself free on earth and was declined. The wicked now bid loves for what repentance once offered gratis. Such is the Day's bitterest arithmetic: infinite tender for what was once had for tears. The verse's brevity suits refusal's finality — three words bid, silence answers. Readers still holding time should hear the bargain inverted: give loves to God now through service, and loves need never be tendered then. Currency accepted today: obedience. Currency accepted then: none. Spend obedience lavishly now, for no currency circulates in that final marketplace.
verses.13:
> their clan that sheltered them

**The Clan That Sheltered Gets Spent**

Faṣīlatihi-llatī tuʾwīh — "his clan that sheltered him." Faṣīlah names the kin-circle — extended family, subtribe, the sheltering ring beyond the household. Tuʾwīh, "gave him refuge," recalls years of protection: blood-money paid, enemies deterred, honor upheld. Now the wicked tender that whole sheltering circle as ransom. Gratitude inverts to expenditure — protectors become payment. The relative clause twists the knife: the clan is bid precisely as shelterer, its sheltering cited on the auction block like provenance on goods. Such is terror's ingratitude. What refuge did for decades gets spent in a verse. Readers should feel loyalty's last fortress fall: household already tendered, now the tribe. Protection purchased with devotion gets sold for survival. The bid will fail, but the bidding itself convicts. Even shelter gets spent by the unsheltered soul.

**Tribe or Mother**

Faṣīlah's sense divides exegetes. Most — Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī — hear the tribe or kin-group, the outer ring of belonging. Some — also reported by Ibn Kathīr and Qatādah — hear the mother, the nearest shelter of infancy. Grounds pull both ways. Tribe fits the auction's widening geometry: children, household, clan, world — each ring larger. Mother fits tuʾwīh's intimacy: none shelter like a mother. Context favors tribe decisively: verse 14's "all on earth" completes an outward expansion, and mother would narrow what must widen. Yet the minority preserves pathos worth keeping — the bidder would spend even her. Strong reading keeps tribe as sense and mother as echo: the clan tendered, maternal love implied in its sheltering. Both agree on the essential — nearest refuge spent. The auction's third ring holds whatever sheltered most.

**Tribalism Meets Its Terminus**

Arabian pride ran on faṣīlah-loyalty — the clan's honor defended unto death, its members ransomed at any price. Earthly auctions ran the opposite direction: clans spent wealth to free members. The Day reverses the market — members spend clans to free themselves. Such inversion ends tribalism as a way to be saved: blood cannot buy what blood never earned. The Book elsewhere voids kinship on that Day — no lineage honored, no intercession unpermitted (23:101 — *“Then, when the Trumpet will be blown, there will be no kinship between them on that Day, nor will they ˹even care to˺ ask about one another”*) — and this verse stages the voiding. Clan-solidarity, noblest of earthly bonds, dissolves into currency.
verses.14:
> and everyone on earth altogether, just to save themselves

**The Whole Planet Goes on the Block**

Wa-man fī-l-arḍi jamīʿan — "all who are on earth, altogether." The auction's final lot: humanity entire, every soul tendered for one skin. Children, spouse, sibling, clan — then the species. Widening completes its geometry: from nearest loves to farthest strangers, all liquidated. "Whoever is on earth" sweeps without exception — righteous and wicked, kin and foreigner, all bid without consent. The bidder auctions what he never owned, spending billions he cannot deliver. Desperation voids property as well as piety. Readers should feel totality's vertigo: the final lot has no number, only a planet. No higher bid exists because no higher belonging does. Earth itself is tendered. Heaven's silence, unbroken across four verses, will break in the next — not with acceptance but with a syllable of refusal.

**What the Living Should Tender Now**

Futility then founds urgency now. The Day takes no ransom, but today takes charity — same wealth, different court. What the wicked will bid in vain, believers can give in profit: feed the hungry now, and no children need bidding then. The sūrah will soon list the righteous who give their wealth's due (70:24-25 — *“and who give the rightful share of their wealth”*), the anti-auction — tendering accepted because tendered in time. Timing is everything: earthly giving purchases heavenly weight; Day's bidding purchases nothing. Readers hold the only currency that will ever count — present obedience. Spend it now or tender loves later. The verse's horror is so pastoral, frightening the living toward generosity. Every dirham given freely today redeems loves that terror would auction tomorrow. Bid now, in charity; the Day's market is closed.
verses.15:
> But no! There will certainly be a raging Flame

**One Syllable Closes the Auction**

Kallā — "nay," "no," "never." One syllable voids four verses of bidding. Most exegetes hear denial of the ransom: no ransom accepted, no bargaining permitted, the auction void. A minority, following Qatādah, hears affirmation — "truly" or "indeed" — pivoting to the fire's certainty. Grounds favor denial: the auction context demands refusal, and kallā typically rebuts what precedes. Yet the minority preserves truth — the fire is indeed certain — folding affirmation into the denial's aftermath. Strong reading keeps denial primary: NO to ransom, then behold the flame. The syllable's brevity is its force; heaven answers planetary bidding with two consonants. Length of pleading meets shortness of verdict. Readers feel the gavel in the gutturals — kallā cracks like a slammed door. Four verses knocked; one syllable bars. Bargaining ends forever.

**Laẓā: The Fire That Churns**

Laẓā names hell by its motion — blazing, churning, leaping fire. The root l-ẓ-y evokes flame's restless flicker; al-Jalālayn derives it from talaẓẓā, to blaze fiercely. This is fire as verb rather than noun — not a place but a devouring. Innahā laẓā, "it is Laẓā," identifies the threat with terrible particularity: not fire generally but this fire, the churning one. Definiteness personalizes torment — Laẓā awaits its own the way hosts await guests. The Book names hell's chambers distinctly (jahannam, saʿīr, saqar, laẓā), and each name preaches: Gehenna the deep, Blaze the fierce, Scorch the searing, Churn the restless. Laẓā's restlessness suits the bidders — their desperation churned through lots; the fire churns through them. Appetite answers appetite. What they fed with loves, the flame feeds with them.
verses.16:
> ripping off scalps

**The Fire Strips Its Prey**

Nazzāʿatan li-l-shawā — "a stripper of scalps." Nazzāʿah intensifies nazʿ, to pull off, tear away, strip — the form (faʿʿālah) means habitual, professional action. Laẓā does not merely burn; it flays, tears, scalps by trade. The feminine agrees with fire (nār), grammatically female, appetite grammatically fixed. Stripping exceeds burning in horror: burns destroy, but stripping removes — skin from skull, covering from core. Exposure compounds pain; the flayed suffer nakedness with searing. Such personification makes fire a butcher rather than element — skilled, repeated, relentless. The verse's three Arabic words hit like hammer-blows: stripper, of, scalps. No verb wasted, no mercy admitted. Readers meet Laẓā at work, not at rest. Naming ended; feeding begins. What the flame does habitually, this verse exhibits once — and once suffices forever.

**The Body Testifies Against Itself**

Flayed flesh preaches fitted recompense. Bodies that served defiance — strong hands hoarding, proud heads scorning, swift feet fleeing truth — get dismantled piece by piece. The Book elsewhere stages limbs testifying: hands speaking, feet witnessing, skins confessing (36:65 — *“On this Day We will seal their mouths, their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will testify to what they used to commit”*; 41:20 — *“When they reach it, their ears, eyes, and skin will testify against what they used to do”*). Laẓā's stripping anticipates that testimony, unmaking the instruments of sin. Hands that withheld charity lose their skin; scalps raised in pride lose their covering. Dismantling is so a moral audit: each removed part answers a misused gift. Readers should inventory their own members — every faculty a trust, every trust an audit. What the fire removes piecemeal, obedience would have preserved whole. The verse anatomizes accountability: bodies are not selves' property but loans. Misused loans get repossessed violently. Keep the scalp by bowing the head; Laẓā scalps only the unbowed.
verses.17:
> It will summon whoever turned their backs ˹on Allah˺ and turned away ˹from the truth˺

**The Fire Has a Voice**

Tadʿū — "it calls" or "summons." Laẓā speaks. After teeth (verse 16's stripping), the flame gains tongue — personification complete. Calling implies knowing: the fire names its own, invites its fuel, summons by appetite. Such voicing terrifies beyond burning — victims hear themselves wanted. The Book elsewhere shows hell conversing — asking for more, answering its keepers — each exchange deepening dread. Voice personalizes what flames generalize: this fire wants you particularly. Summoning also inverts mercy's call — prophets summoned to life, Laẓā summons to ruin. Two invitations span every biography; each soul RSVPs by conduct. Readers hear both calls now, prophets' through scripture and Laẓā's through warning. Answer the first, and the second never names you. The fire's voice is warning's echo — heed the echo's Sender, escape the echo.

**Summoned, Not Dragged — Yet**

Calling precedes seizure. Laẓā summons before it grips — dread of approach seasoning pain of arrival. Such sequencing prolongs torment psychologically: hearing one's name, watching others taken, awaiting the grip. Anticipation tortures before contact begins. The verse stages only the call; dragging belongs to darker verses (chains in 69:30-32 — *“˹It will be said,˺ “Seize and shackle them then burn them in Hell then tie them up with chains seventy arms long”* will show it). Pacing serves dread's crescendo — voice, then hands. Readers should feel the interval: summoned and standing, called but not yet claimed. That interval, mercifully brief in text, stretches eternally in experience. Warnings work the same way now — calls before consequences. Heed the call's content (turn back!) and never hear its sequel. The fire that calls its own also, through scripture, warns its potential. Answer in repentance.
verses.18:
> and gathered and hoarded ˹wealth˺

**Wealth Gathered, Mercy Scattered**

Jamaʿa fa-awʿā — "gathered and stored." Jamaʿa piles up; awʿā stows away — accumulation plus retention, earning plus embalming. Wiʿāʾ, the noun behind the verb, means vessel, container: the hoarder turns wealth into contents sealed from circulation. Gathering serves life; hoarding serves fear — fear of poverty, of future, of dependence on God. The fa- links piling to storing as habit: gathered, therefore stowed; earned, therefore entombed. Such pairing indicts not possession but posture — hands open to receive, closed to release. Wealth's purpose is flow: provision through the rich to the poor. Hoarding dams the flow, flooding the hoarder while parching neighbors. Readers audit their vessels: does wealth pass through toward need, or pool behind fear? Containers confess. What you store against God, Laẓā counts as fuel.

**The Twin Verse in Sūrah 104**

Sūrah 104 opens on the same figure: the slandering backbiter who amasses wealth and tallies it (104:1-2 — *“who amasses wealth ˹greedily˺ and counts it ˹repeatedly˺”*). Twin portraits, twin dooms — gathering-plus-counting there, gathering-plus-storing here. The pairing instructs: hoarding's sociology (slander guards wealth; wealth funds pride) meets hoarding's the teaching about the Last Day (Laẓā summons both). Counting deserves note — the 104 hoarder numbers his piles, affection quantified. Numbers replace neighbors; tallies replace ties. Together the verses anatomize miserliness whole: mouth wounding (slander), hands clutching (hoarding), heart counting (tallying). Laẓā claims the complete figure — back turned on truth (verse 17), hands closed to poor (verse 18), tongue loose on fellows (104).

**Hoarding Means Withholding Zakāh**

Exegetes specify the crime: refusing the obligatory alms, zakāh — the poor's due portion in the rich's wealth. Hoarding here is not mere saving but withholding what God assigned others. The poor own a share of every fortune; the hoarder expropriates it. A blistering tableau elsewhere details the wage: hoarded gold and silver heated in hellfire, branding foreheads, sides, and backs — "taste what you hoarded" (9:34-35). Branding fits hoarding part by part: foreheads that frowned at beggars, sides turned away, backs presented. Such fittingness preaches proportion — members that withheld get marked. Readers should translate doctrine to dirhams: zakāh calculated, zakāh paid, conscience clear. The verse threatens not wealth but theft-from-God. What He earmarked for the poor was never yours. Withhold it, and Laẓā collects with interest.
verses.19:
> Indeed, humankind was created impatient

**Anxiety Is Built In**

Khuliqa — "was created." Halūʿan — "anxious, fretful, grasping." The passive verb assigns constitution: humanity comes off the line impatient. Qatādah glosses halūʿ as greed-plus-covetousness-plus-severe-anxiety — a compound frailty, clutching and fretting at once. Such built-in-ness forbids despair and excuses nothing: nature explains struggle without excusing surrender. The verse diagnoses, not absolves — doctors name diseases to prescribe cures. Halūʿ's breadth matters: impatience here spans haste, greed, panic, and stinginess — the whole syndrome verses 20-21 will split. Readers should receive the diagnosis as self-knowledge: this is your factory setting. Grace does not deny the setting; it retrains it. What creation wired, revelation rewires — patience commanded (verse 5), prayer prescribed (verse 22). Nature proposes anxiety; obedience disposes.

**Haste Across Three Verses**

The Book returns to human haste repeatedly: created of haste (21:37 — *“Humankind is made of haste. I will soon show you My signs, so do not ask Me to hasten them”*), ever hasty in judgment (17:11 — *“And humans ˹swiftly˺ pray for evil as they pray for good. For humankind is ever hasty”*), created anxious here. Three verses, one trait — impatience as humanity's signature flaw. Each instance targets a facet: 21:37 — *“Humankind is made of haste. I will soon show you My signs, so do not ask Me to hasten them”* mocks demanding signs quickly; 17:11 — *“And humans ˹swiftly˺ pray for evil as they pray for good. For humankind is ever hasty”* warns praying for evil as for good; this verse anatomizes fret-and-grudge. Together they map haste whole: hasty wants, hasty prayers, hasty temper. Repetition across sūrahs signals centrality — this flaw, above others, needs naming. Haste explains the challenger's dare (verse 1: punish now!), the auction's panic (verses 11-14: save me now!), and hoarding's clutch (verse 18: keep now!). One root, many fruits. Readers tracing their faults to haste find the Book's agreement. Slow down, and half the sins starve. Patience is not one virtue among many — it is impatience's scheduled executioner.
verses.20:
> distressed when touched with evil

*Idhā massahu al-sharru jazūʿā* — when evil touches him, he panics. The word *jazūʿ* is not ordinary sadness; it is the shrillness of a person whose composure breaks the moment something goes wrong, and *massahu* — touched him — makes the affliction as light as a touch. The Book draws the portrait in two brush-strokes here and in the next verse: distress when touched with harm, withholding when touched with good. Between them they describe a life organised entirely around the moment, with no horizon long enough to hold either grief or gratitude. What follows in the sūrah names the exception — those who pray (70:22 — *“except those who pray”*) — and the list of their qualities is best read as the cure for exactly this temperament: constancy in prayer, a share of wealth set aside, chastity, honesty about trusts. A fear that keeps a person from assuming he is safe.
verses.21:
> and withholding when touched with good—

*Wa-idhā massahu al-khayru manūʿā* — and when good touches him, he hoards. The pairing with the previous verse is deliberate: the same man who cannot bear a loss also cannot share a gain, and the two failures come from the same root, which is a self with nothing larger than itself in view. *Manūʿ* is the person who withholds as a matter of habit, and the Book uses the noun for this disposition in the description of the stingy, who when good comes to them are grudging (17:83 — *“When We grant people Our favours, they turn away, acting arrogantly. But when touched with evil, they lose all hope”* is the same pairing: despairing and ungrateful). The cure stated in the verses that follow is not a mood but a practice: *ḥaqq maʿlūm*, a determined share of the wealth set aside for the beggar and the deprived (70:24–25 — *“and who give the rightful share of their wealth”*). The sūrah does not ask the hoarder to feel generous; it asks him to open his hand on schedule.
verses.22:
> except those who pray

*Illā al-muṣallīn* — except those who pray. The exception is the hinge of the whole passage: the portrait of 70:19–21 — *“Indeed, humankind was created impatient distressed when touched with evil and withholding when touched with good”* is a general human condition, and the one thing that marks out the people who escape it is not intelligence, courage, or wealth, but prayer. The Book makes the same claim in its first sūrah, where the straight path is asked for by people who will be found among those who pray, and it identifies restraint of the appetites with prayer elsewhere: prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing (29:45 — *“Indeed, ˹genuine˺ prayer should deter ˹one˺ from indecency and wickedness.”*). The list that follows — 70:23–35 — *“consistently performing their prayers”* — expands the single word into its parts, and the two ends of the list are prayer itself (70:23 — *“consistently performing their prayers”*, 70:34 — *“and who are ˹properly˺ observant of their prayers”*), which frames everything in between. The sūrah treats prayer as a life-organising act rather than a ritual moment, and the frame of the list is how it says so.

---

The exception is the pivot of the passage: the sūrah has drawn the portrait of a human being who is impatient, faint-hearted when harm comes and withholding when good comes, and the one thing that marks out the exception is the prayer that follows. The same construction appears in the sūrah of the Believers, where the description of the believers' qualities opens with the phrase "those who are humble in their prayers" (23:1–2), and in the sūrah of the Believers' passage on the inheritors of the Garden, whose list also begins with prayer. The list of nine qualities that follows this verse is the sūrah's description of what prayer produces, so the prayer here is both the entry and the root.
verses.23:
> consistently performing their prayers

*Alladhīna hum ʿalā ṣalātihim dāʾimūn* — those who are constant in their prayers. The word *dāʾimūn* describes steady persistence rather than an unbroken act: the Book uses it for the quality of a life, not for a ritual that never ends. It is the same characteristic the Book gives the believers later in this sūrah with a different word — those who guard their prayers (70:34 — *“and who are ˹properly˺ observant of their prayers”*) — which is why the two verses form the frame of the list, opening and closing the qualities named. The Book links this constancy to protection in the Hereafter and to the structure of the day: it commands prayer at the two ends of the daylight and in the first hours of the night (11:114 — *“Establish prayer ˹O Prophet˺ at both ends of the day and in the early part of the night. Surely good deeds wipe out evil deeds. That is a reminder for the mindful”*). It describes the believers' prayer in the middle of a night vigil they maintain in turns (73:20 — *“He knows that you ˹believers˺ are unable to endure this, and has turned to you in mercy.”*). What the verse praises is not intensity but reliability.
verses.24:
> and who give the rightful share of their wealth

*Wa-alladhīna fī amwālihim ḥaqqun maʿlūm* — and in whose wealth there is a determined right. The right is *maʿlūm*, known and specified, not left to the mood of the owner or to the appeal of the poor: the Book treats charity here as a standing claim on property rather than an occasional generosity. The Qur'an states the same claim in Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt, where the wealth of the righteous has a share for the beggar and the deprived (51:19 — *“And in their wealth there was a rightful share ˹fulfilled˺ for the beggar and the poor”*), and it makes the poor a right-holder elsewhere: give the relative his right, and the needy and the traveller (30:38 — *“So give your close relatives their due, as well as the poor and the ˹needy˺ traveller.”*). This is the answer to the hoarder of 70:21 — *“and withholding when touched with good”*, and the answer given is structural — a share carved out before the appetite can be consulted. The following verse names the two recipients, so that the size and target of the share are clear.
verses.25:
> to the beggar and the poor

*Li-al-sāʾili wa-al-maḥrūm* — for the one who asks and the one who is deprived. The two words divide poverty into its visible and hidden kinds. *Sāʾil* is the person who puts out his hand and makes his need known; *maḥrūm* is the one who has been held back from provision — the poor man who does not ask, the widow, the orphan, the family whose dignity keeps them silent. The Book names the same pair in 51:19 — *“And in their wealth there was a rightful share ˹fulfilled˺ for the beggar and the poor”*, and it instructs the Prophet to refuse to turn away the one who asks (93:10 — *“nor repulse the beggar”*). The pairing is the reason the verse says the right is *known*: a charity that only answers a request would leave out everyone too proud or too frightened to speak, so the share has to be determined by the giver's knowledge rather than by the poor man's courage. This is the second quality in the sūrah's list, and it stands directly against the grasping of 70:21 — *“and withholding when touched with good”*.
verses.26:
> and who ˹firmly˺ believe in the Day of Judgment

The description of the successful worshippers fills this passage (70:22–35 — *“except those who pray”*), and belief in the Day of Judgement is one of its marks. The pairing with prayer is deliberate: a person prays to a God who will judge, and the two beliefs stand or fall together, which is why the Book says in many places that denying the reckoning is what makes people reckless (74:46 — *“and deny the Day of Judgment”*; 82:9 — *“But no! In fact, you deny the ˹final˺ Judgment”*). The passage lists the believers' qualities in the plural — constancy in prayer, a share of wealth for the beggar, chastity, keeping trusts, standing by testimony — and this verse is one of the grounds the others rest on.
verses.27:
> and those who fear the punishment of their Lord—

*Wa-alladhīna hum min ʿadhābi rabbihim mushfiqūn* — and those who are anxious about the punishment of their Lord. *Shafaqah* is a fear that is mixed with care, the apprehension of someone who has not forgotten what is at stake, and the Book uses it for the state it praises in the believers (21:90 — *“So We answered his prayer, granted him John, and made his wife fertile. Indeed, they used to race in doing good, and call upon Us with hope and fear, totally humbling themselves before Us”*; 23:57 — *“Surely those who tremble in awe of their Lord”*). This quality is not the same as doubt about God's mercy: the very next verse states explicitly that no one should feel secure from the punishment of his Lord (70:28 — *“˹knowing that˺ none should feel secure from their Lord’s punishment”*), which means the fear named here is the companion of hope, not its rival. The Book describes the same balance elsewhere when it speaks of a people who call on God in hope and fear (32:16 — *“They abandon their beds, invoking their Lord with hope and fear, and donate from what We have provided for them”*), and it makes this watchfulness one of the marks by which the successful are known in Sūrah al-Muʾminūn (23:57–61 — *“Surely those who tremble in awe of their Lord and who believe in the revelations of their Lord and who associate none with their Lord and who do whatever ˹good˺ they do with their hearts fearful, ˹knowing˺ that they will return to their Lord— it is they who race to do good deeds, always taking the lead”*). The contrast inside the sūrah is worth noticing: the mockers demanded the punishment at once (70:1 — *“A challenger has demanded a punishment bound to come”*), while these believers live as though it could arrive at any moment.
verses.28:
> ˹knowing that˺ none should feel secure from their Lord’s punishment—

**No One Is Safe From It**

The verse completes the description of the servants of the Merciful who pray: they are those who "give what they give while their hearts tremble" — and, as this verse says, they know that *ʿadhāba rabbihim ghayru maʾmūn*, that no one is safe from their Lord's punishment. The Arabic negates the idea of security itself: it is not that some are exempt and others are not, but that no one may presume on immunity.

Sūrah al-Furqān states the same in the prayer of the servants: "Keep away from us the punishment of Hell — indeed its punishment is ever adhering" (25:65). The verse is not despair. Faith works between fear and hope, and this line supplies the fear that keeps hope honest. The history in this Book shows what happens when the other balance is lost. ʿĀd felt safe in their well-watered valleys and were taken by a screaming wind (69:6–7 — *“And as for ’Ȃd, they were destroyed by a furious, bitter wind which Allah unleashed on them non-stop for seven nights and eight days, so that you would have seen its people lying dead like trunks of uprooted palm trees”*); Thamūd felt safe behind their carved cliffs and were taken by a blast (7:78 — *“Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them, and they fell lifeless in their homes”*); Pharaoh felt safe with the Nile at his command and was taken by the sea (7:136 — *“So We inflicted punishment upon them, drowning them in the sea for denying Our signs and being heedless of them”*). Each of them treated security as a right. The servants of the Merciful treat it as a presumption, and so they keep praying.
verses.29:
> and those who guard their chastity

*Wa-alladhīna hum li-furūjihim ḥāfiẓūn* — and those who guard their chastity. The Book states this quality in almost the same words in Sūrah al-Muʾminūn, where the believers are described as guarding their private parts except with their spouses, and the passage there ends with the same conclusion as here: whoever seeks beyond that is a transgressor (23:5–7 — *“those who guard their chastity”*). The phrasing is deliberately about guarding rather than about abstaining, which fits the whole sūrah's understanding of the virtues as disciplines maintained rather than states achieved. The Book pairs chastity with prayer in this list and gives the reason elsewhere: modesty is part of faith, and the eye is where it begins (24:30–31 — *“And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and guard their chastity, and not to reveal their adornments except what normally appears.”*). The next verse states the limit that makes the guard possible — the lawful, and nothing beyond it.
verses.30:
> except with their wives or those ˹bondwomen˺ in their possession, for then they are free from blame

*Illā ʿalā azwājihim aw mā malakat aymānuhum* — except with their spouses or those whom their right hands possess. The Book's formula here is the same one used in the two other sūrahs that describe the believers (23:6 — *“except with their wives or those ˹bondwomen˺ in their possession, for then they are free from blame”*; 33:50 — *“O Prophet! We have made lawful for you your wives to whom you have paid their ˹full˺ dowries as well as those ˹bondwomen˺ in your possession, whom Allah has granted you.”*), and it sets the boundary of the guarded life: the discipline of the previous verse is not asceticism but the channel of the lawful. The Qur'an never presents desire itself as the problem. What it forbids is the crossing of the stated line, which is why the sentence is constructed as an exception rather than a prohibition. The Book also names the purpose of marriage in these terms elsewhere — that spouses find tranquillity in one another and God places affection and mercy between them (30:21 — *“And He has placed between you compassion and mercy.”*) — so that the verse's permission is not a concession to appetite but the design the appetite is meant to serve. The following verse names the cost of going past it.
verses.31:
> but whoever seeks beyond that are the transgressors

*Fa-mani ibtaghā warāʾa dhālika fa-ulāʾika humu al-ʿādūn* — and whoever seeks beyond that, those are the transgressors. *ʿĀdūn* is built on the root of crossing a boundary, and it is the same word the Book uses for aggression and for stepping over the limits of God (2:229 — *“And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, they are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers”*; 65:1 — *“And whoever transgresses Allah’s limits has truly wronged his own soul.”*). So the sentence does not describe an excess of desire but a violation of a limit, and it closes the discussion of chastity with a legal verdict rather than a moral complaint. The Book states the same conclusion in the same terms at the end of the parallel passage in Sūrah al-Muʾminūn (23:7 — *“but whoever seeks beyond that are the transgressors”*), which is one of the clearest signals that this list of qualities is a known type in the Qur'an and not a sequence written for this sūrah alone. The transgressor here is not the man with strong feeling but the man with no boundary.
verses.32:
> ˹The faithful are˺ also those who are true to their trusts and covenants

*Wa-alladhīna hum li-amānātihim wa-ʿahdihim rāʿūn* — and those who keep their trusts and their covenant. The two words cover the whole field of obligations a person carries: *amānāt* are the things entrusted to him — money, secrets, authority, a child, a position — and *ʿahd* is the word he has given, whether to God or to another human being. The Book stresses this duty at the head of Sūrah al-Muʾminūn, where the believers are described as faithful to their trusts and promises (23:8 — *“˹the believers are also˺ those who are true to their trusts and covenants”*), and it names breach of covenant as one of the marks of the hypocrite in the Prophet's teaching — the three signs he listed are that when a man speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is trusted he betrays (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 33). The Book also ties it to the public order: it commands that the trusts be delivered to their owners and that judgement be given with justice (4:58 — *“Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners; and when you judge between people, judge with fairness.”*), which is why the quality belongs in a list of what makes a community possible, between chastity and testimony.

**The Trust and the Covenant**

The verse is one item in the sūrah's portrait of the believers that runs from 70:22 — *“except those who pray”* to 70:35 — *“These will be in Gardens, held in honour”*. The list includes constant prayer, the right of the beggar and the deprived in a person's wealth, the fear of the Day, chastity, and this entry: those who keep their trusts and their covenant. The two words cover most of a person's dealings. A trust is what is placed in a person's hand and not seen by any other hand, and a covenant is a promise a person has made and can break quietly. The Book names both in the same command elsewhere, ordering the believers to hand back what they hold in trust and to judge with justice (4:58 — *“Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners; and when you judge between people, judge with fairness.”*), and the Sūrah of the Night Journey warns that every covenant will be questioned (17:34 — *“Do not come near the wealth of the orphan—unless intending to enhance it—until they attain maturity. Honour ˹your˺ pledges, for you will surely be accountable for them”*).
**The Weight the Word Carries**

The Book calls the trust *al-amānah* and describes it in a way that raises the stakes: the heavens and the earth and the mountains were offered it and declined, and the human being took it on (33:72 — *“Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they ˹all˺ declined to bear it, being fearful of it.”*). The scholars read the trust in that verse as the obligations of the law, and the passage in front of us shows it in the small form: the object left with a neighbour, the money entrusted to a partner, the promise made in a moment of enthusiasm. Bukhārī and Muslim report the Prophet's description of the signs of the hypocrite, and the first two are that he lies when he speaks and breaks a promise when he makes one.
**Why It Is in This List**

The sūrah is closing with a portrait of the people who will be honoured in the gardens (70:35 — *“These will be in Gardens, held in honour”*), and the list is not a set of heroic deeds. It is a set of habits: praying, giving, guarding, keeping. The verse before this one speaks of those who are constant in their testimony, and the verse after it names the guarding of prayer. The reason the trust stands next to prayer in the list is the sūrah's own understanding of religion: what a person does with what nobody is watching is the same thing as what he does in the mosque.
verses.33:
> and who are honest in their testimony

**Seventh Duty: True Testimony**

Wa-lladhīna hum bi-shahādātihim qāʾimūn — "and those who stand firm by their testimonies." Shahādāt (plural) covers every testimony: courtroom oaths, witnessed contracts, character references, even informal accounts of events. Qāʾimūn means standing, upright, firmly established — testimony delivered standing straight, without bending toward bribes or buckling under threats. Such uprightness extends verse 32's fidelity from deeds to words: trusts guarded in action, truth guarded in speech. The list progresses outward through the believer's life — prayer, wealth, conviction, dread, body, trusts — and now reaches the tongue in its most solemn function. False testimony destroys precisely what trusts build: justice, confidence, social order. Readers should treat every testimony as worship: oaths sworn truthfully, accounts given accurately, references written honestly. What tongues testify under pressure, character proves. Stand witnesses upright; never bend testimony. Seventh duty: truth standing.

**Standing Firm Against Pressure**

Qiyām means standing — and standing implies pressure to sit, to bend, to fall. Witnesses face bribes from the rich, threats from the powerful, pleas from kin. "Stand firm for justice as witnesses for Allah, even against yourselves, your parents, or your kin" (paraphrased from 4:135 — *“O believers! Stand firm for justice as witnesses for Allah even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or close relatives.”*). Such firmness costs: testifying against family fractures gatherings, testifying against patrons ends patronage. Yet the verse commands standing precisely there — where sitting profits. Pressure tests testimony's object: witnesses for Allah stand, witnesses for advantage bend. The upright witness fears only the final cross-examination, where tongues testify against their owners. Readers should pre-decide firmness: resolve now to testify truly regardless of parties. What pressure bends in life, fire straightens in torment. Stand against kin if truth demands; never bend for kin if falsehood asks. Pressure reveals witnesses; firmness defines them.

**False Witness Corrodes Justice**

False testimony ranks among the gravest sins because it weaponizes justice's own machinery. Courts depend on witnesses; lying witnesses turn acquittal into condemnation and theft into title. "Those who do not testify falsely" (paraphrased from 25:72 — *“˹They are˺ those who do not bear false witness, and when they come across falsehood, they pass ˹it˺ by with dignity”*) — the merciful Lord's servants defined partly by this refusal. Such refusal protects the vulnerable most: the poor cannot buy witnesses, the stranger cannot summon crowds. One false oath can hang the innocent, free the guilty, orphan children of inheritance. Corrosion spreads beyond single cases: known perjury teaches communities that oaths are theater.
verses.34:
> and who are ˹properly˺ observant of their prayers

*Wa-alladhīna hum ʿalā ṣalātihim yuḥāfiẓūn* — and those who guard their prayers. The list that opened with constancy in prayer (70:23 — *“consistently performing their prayers”*) closes with vigilance over it, and the change of word is deliberate: *dāʾim*, steady, describes the habit, while *yuḥāfiẓūn*, keeping watch, describes the care that protects the habit from slipping into routine. The Book uses the same verb for guarding the private parts in this passage (70:29 — *“and those who guard their chastity”*) and for keeping the bounds God has set (2:238 — *“Observe the ˹five obligatory˺ prayers—especially the middle prayer—and stand in true devotion to Allah”*), so the two ends of the list hold the same discipline in two tenses: the practice, and the attention that keeps the practice alive. Practically, the scholars read the verse as covering the conditions, timing, and spirit of the prayer, not only the performance of it. The next verse names the reward promised to the people described in all eleven clauses.
verses.35:
> These will be in Gardens, held in honour

*Ulāʾika fī jannātin mukramūn* — those will be in gardens, held in honour. The demonstrative *ulāʾika* gathers every quality named in the passage and answers them in a single promise, and *mukramūn* is the Book's word for being received with honour rather than for being rewarded: the same word describes the angels as honoured servants of God (80:16 — *“honourable and virtuous”*; see also 51:24–27 — *“Has the story of Abraham’s honoured guests reached you ˹O Prophet˺ ˹Remember˺ when they entered his presence and greeted ˹him with˺, “Peace!” He replied, “Peace ˹be upon you˺!” ˹Then he said to himself,˺ “˹These are˺ an unfamiliar people.” Then he slipped off to his family and brought a fat ˹roasted˺ calf and placed it before them, asking, “Will you not eat?”*). So the reward is stated in the language of welcome, which is consistent with the sūrah's treatment of the believers' qualities as the preparation of a guest. The Book uses the same word in the description of the Prophet's own station when it speaks of a generous provision (37:41 — *“They will have a known provision”*) and of the reward of the righteous (36:27 — *“of how my Lord has forgiven me, and made me one of the honourable.”*). The contrast with the mockers of the next verses is the point of the change of subject: the list is finished, and the sūrah turns to the men who were ridiculing the very promise it has just described.
verses.36:
> So what is the matter with the disbelievers that they rush ˹head-long˺ towards you ˹O Prophet˺

*Fa-māli alladhīna kafarū qibalaka muhṭiʿīn* — so what is the matter with the disbelievers that they rush headlong towards you? The image is of a crowd leaning and stretching towards the Prophet from every side, craning their necks to see him — not to listen but to mock, as the next verse makes explicit. The Book's question is a rebuke in the form of astonishment: what do they think they will find? The verse follows the promise of the gardens with honour (70:35 — *“These will be in Gardens, held in honour”*) and precedes the question about whether every one of them expects to be admitted to such a garden (70:38 — *“Does every one of them expect to be admitted into a Garden of Bliss”*), which is the answer. The scene matches what the Book records about the Quraysh gathering around the Prophet in rings to heckle (6:5 — *“They have indeed rejected the truth when it came to them, so they will soon face the consequences of their ridicule”*; 17:47–48 — *“See how they call you names ˹O Prophet˺! So they have gone so ˹far˺ astray that they cannot find the ˹Right˺ Way”*), and it is the last picture of the disbelievers before the sūrah turns to the Day.
verses.37:
> from the right and the left, in groups ˹to mock you˺

*ʿAni al-yamīni wa-ʿani al-shimāli ʿizīn* — from the right and from the left, in factions. The picture is of crowds gathered round the Prophet in groups and parties, listening in order to mock rather than to learn; the word *ʿizīn* carries the sense of companies and bands, each with its own opinion and its own amusement. The next verse answers them with a question: does every one of them hope to enter a garden of bliss? The Book records the same stance in Sūrah al-Hijr, where the incoming visitors turn away and mock when the truth reaches them (15:11–13 — *“but no messenger ever came to them without being mocked This is how We allow disbelief ˹to steep˺ into the hearts of the wicked They would not believe in this ˹Quran˺ despite the ˹many˺ examples of those ˹destroyed˺ before”*), and in Sūrah al-Muṭaffifīn, where the believers' faith was treated as a standing joke (83:29–32 — *“Indeed, the wicked used to laugh at the believers wink to one another whenever they passed by and muse ˹over these exploits˺ upon returning to their own people And when they saw the faithful, they would say, “These ˹people˺ are truly astray,”*). The scene is a reminder of what the Prophet faced from his own city, and the sūrah's answer to it is not a defence but a question about what the mockers expect for themselves.
verses.38:
> Does every one of them expect to be admitted into a Garden of Bliss

*A-yuṭmaʿu kullu imriʾin minhum an yudkhala jannata naʿīm* — does every one of them hope to be admitted to a garden of bliss? The question lands after the picture of the crowd craning and laughing (70:36–37 — *“So what is the matter with the disbelievers that they rush ˹head-long˺ towards you ˹O Prophet˺ from the right and the left, in groups ˹to mock you˺”*), and its answer is the reminder that follows: God knows what He created them from (70:39 — *“But no! Indeed, they ˹already˺ know what We created them from”*). The sūrah does not say that they hope for paradise; it asks whether they do, and leaves the mockers to hear themselves. The Book asks the same kind of question elsewhere, where it points out the contradiction between treating the message as a joke and expecting its reward (23:84–90 — *“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “To whom belong the earth and all those on it, if you ˹really˺ know?”*). The verse also serves the structure of the sūrah: the description of the believers ended with gardens and honour (70:35 — *“These will be in Gardens, held in honour”*), so the question measures the distance between the two audiences — one list, one destination, and a crowd in the middle laughing at both.
verses.39:
> But no! Indeed, they ˹already˺ know what We created them from

*Kallā* — no indeed. The answer to the crowd's hope of paradise (70:38 — *“Does every one of them expect to be admitted into a Garden of Bliss”*) is the reminder of their origin: *innā khalaqnāhum mimmā yaʿlamūn*, We created them from what they know. A creature made from a drop of fluid, who will return to dust, should think twice before treating the promise of resurrection as ridiculous. The Book uses this argument repeatedly: the God who made the first creation can make the second (36:79–81 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “They will be revived by the One Who produced them the first time, for He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of every created being”*; 46:33 — *“Do they not realize that Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth and did not tire in creating them, is able to give life to the dead? Yes ˹indeed˺! He is certainly Most Capable of everything”*; 75:37–40 — *“Were they not ˹once˺ a sperm-drop emitted Then they became a clinging clot ˹of blood˺, then He developed and perfected their form producing from it both sexes, male and female Is such ˹a Creator˺ unable to bring the dead back to life”*). Pride about lineage and standing collapses in front of the question of what a person is made of.

**Where the Argument Comes From**

The verse answers the question that opens this closing passage: does every one of these people hope to be admitted into a garden of delight? (70:38 — *“Does every one of them expect to be admitted into a Garden of Bliss”*). The men raising the question were the same crowd that pressed the Prophet from the right and the left, expecting to be included in the promise while keeping their own gods (70:36-37 — *“from the right and the left, in groups ˹to mock you˺”*). The answer is their raw material. A creature made from a drop of fluid and headed for the dust does not get to treat the raising of the dead as an impossibility. The sūrah has just finished its portrait of the people who will actually be honoured: constant in prayer, careful with trusts, honest in testimony, and watchful of their prayers (70:22-35 — *“except those who pray consistently performing their prayers and who give the rightful share of their wealth to the beggar and the poor and who ˹firmly˺ believe in the Day of Judgment and those who fear the punishment of their Lord— ˹knowing that˺ none should feel secure from their Lord’s punishment— and those who guard their chastity except with their wives or those ˹bondwomen˺ in their possession, for then they are free from blame”*), and the point of the contrast is that the promise was never distributed by tribe or by confidence.
verses.40:
> So, I do swear by the Lord of ˹all˺ the points of sunrise and sunset that We are truly capable

*Fa-lā uqsimu bi-rabbi al-mashāriqi wa-al-maghārib* — the oath is by the Lord of every place of sunrise and sunset, put in the plural, which covers the shifting points of the year: the measure is His and so is the power behind it. The oath stands before a statement of capability in the next verse, and it answers the mockers a few lines earlier — the God who keeps the orbits running can replace them, and can raise the dead.
