The same oath appears at 37:5 — *“˹He is˺ the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, and the Lord of all points of sunrise”* and 55:17 — *“˹He is˺ Lord of the two easts and the two wests”*, and the argument is always the same: the order of the skies is the evidence.

**What the Oath Is Doing**

An oath in the Book is not decoration. It is placed in front of a claim that the hearer was resisting, and here the claim is that God is able to replace these mockers with better people (70:41 — *“of replacing them with ˹others˺ better than them, and We cannot be prevented ˹from doing so˺”*). The oath is taken by the Lord of the places of sunrise and sunset, and the plural matters: not one sunrise and one sunset but all of them, the points where the sun comes up and goes down through the year, shifting as the seasons shift. Whoever keeps those moving has an easy time with a grave. The Book swears by the same horizons in the sūrah of the Ranks (37:5 — *“˹He is˺ the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, and the Lord of all points of sunrise”*) and again in the Most Merciful, where the two easts and the two wests are named (55:17 — *“˹He is˺ Lord of the two easts and the two wests”*), and the argument in each place is that order visible to everybody is evidence of the One who made it.
verses.41:
> of replacing them with ˹others˺ better than them, and We cannot be prevented ˹from doing so˺

*An nubaddila khayran minhum wa mā naḥnu bi-masbūqīn* — to exchange them for better people, and no one can outrun Us. The verse states plainly what the Book implies throughout: a community that receives a revelation is not irreplaceable, and its failure does not defeat what God has planned. The Qur'an says the same at 47:38 — *“Here you are, being invited to donate ˹a little˺ in the cause of Allah. Still some of you withhold. And whoever does so, it is only to their own loss. For Allah is the Self-Sufficient, whereas you stand in need ˹of Him˺. If you ˹still˺ turn away, He will replace you with another people. And they will not be like you”* and 5:54 — *“O believers! Whoever among you abandons their faith, Allah will replace them with others who love Him and are loved by Him. They will be humble with the believers but firm towards the disbelievers, struggling in the Way of Allah; fearing no blame from anyone. This is the favour of Allah. He grants it to whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing”*, where a people are told that others will be brought in their place. *Masbūqīn*, overtaken or outrun, denies any escape from the decree. For the mockers in this passage the threat is not only punishment but substitution: the message will find its people.

---

The power to replace a people is the same threat the sūrah of the Spoils states to the community that fails to march: God will replace them with others who will not be like them (9:39 — *“If you do not march forth, He will afflict you with a painful torment and replace you with other people.”*), and the sūrah of the Table puts the possibility in the positive form: God is not in need of a community, and He can bring a people whom He will love and who will love Him (5:54 — *“O believers! Whoever among you abandons their faith, Allah will replace them with others who love Him and are loved by Him.”*). What the verse's phrase forbids is the notion that the arrangement is fixed in the community's favour: the Book speaks of provision, of prophecy and of victory as gifts entrusted rather than possessed, and the closing words, that no one can outrun Him, close the question.
verses.42:
> So let them indulge ˹in falsehood˺ and amuse ˹themselves˺ until they face their Day, which they have been threatened with—

*Fa-dharhum yakhūḍū wa yalʿabū* — leave them to wade and to play. The command is given to the Prophet, and the same instruction appears at 43:83 — *“So let them indulge ˹in falsehood˺ and amuse ˹themselves˺ until they face their Day, which they have been warned of”* and 6:91 — *“And they have not shown Allah His proper reverence when they said, “Allah has revealed nothing to any human being.”*: the answer to mockery is not to spend the message on people who have decided to amuse themselves with it. They are left to their distraction until the day they were promised, and the next verses describe the coming that ends it. The verse holds the Book's patience and its severity together: the time for play is short, and it stops without ceremony. The mercy inside the delay is stated elsewhere — time is given so that they might return (32:21 — *“We will certainly make them taste some of the minor torment ˹in this life˺ before the major torment ˹of the Hereafter˺, so perhaps they will return ˹to the Right Path˺”*).

**The Command and Its Limits**

The command tells the Prophet to leave them to it: to wade, to play, to talk, until they meet the day they were promised. The sūrah of the Ornament repeats the phrase and adds the day itself, when they will be told what they used to do (43:83 — *“So let them indulge ˹in falsehood˺ and amuse ˹themselves˺ until they face their Day, which they have been warned of”*), and the Sūrah of the Cattle gives the same answer to another set of mockers (6:91 — *“And they have not shown Allah His proper reverence when they said, “Allah has revealed nothing to any human being.”*). The Book hands this instruction to a man being insulted daily, and it is not permission to stop caring. It is a statement of where his responsibility ends. A messenger delivers and explains; the wading is the hearers' own business, and the delay is not a gap in the plan. The Book says elsewhere that the time is given so that people might return (32:21 — *“We will certainly make them taste some of the minor torment ˹in this life˺ before the major torment ˹of the Hereafter˺, so perhaps they will return ˹to the Right Path˺”*; 35:45 — *“If Allah were to punish people ˹immediately˺ for what they have committed, He would not have left a single living being on earth. But He delays them for an appointed term. And when their time arrives, then surely Allah is All-Seeing of His servants”*), and this verse shows what happens when the time runs out.
verses.43:
> the Day they will come forth from the graves swiftly, as if racing to an idol ˹for a blessing˺

*Yawma yakhrujūna min al-ajdāthī sirāʿan* — the word for their hurrying is the one the Book uses for people rushing to the stone of their idols, and that is the comparison the verse draws. The resurrection gets the speed of something they already did in the world: former idolaters ran to their shrines, and now they run from their graves towards the reckoning. The verse before this one left them playing; this one shows the game ended. Their haste is no longer devotion but compulsion, which is why the next line describes them with their eyes downcast and disgrace covering them.

**The Comparison the Word Carries**

The word for their coming out is *sirāʿan*, the running pace of people heading for something they want, and the Book uses the same idea the sūrah of the Moon states: the day they come out of the graves like scattered locusts, hurrying towards the caller (54:7-8 — *“rushing towards the caller. The disbelievers will cry, “This is a difficult Day!”*). The second half of the verse makes the comparison sharper by naming what they used to rush towards — the standing stones and shrines they went to in the world, which the Qur'an calls *nasaṣb*. The same legs and the same hurry, aimed at something else. The sūrah of Yā Sīn gives the same scene in a quieter line, with the dead coming out to their Lord (36:51 — *“The Trumpet will be blown ˹a second time˺, then—behold!—they will rush from the graves to their Lord”*), and the difference between the two pictures is only where the running leads.
verses.44:
> with eyes downcast, utterly covered with disgrace. That is the Day they have ˹always˺ been warned of

*Khāshiʿatan abṣāruhum tarhaquhum dhillah* — their gaze lowered and disgrace covering them. The Book often describes the people of the Fire this way, because the lowering of the eyes is the gesture of the proud finally undone (see 68:43 — *“with eyes downcast, totally covered with disgrace. For they were ˹always˺ called to prostrate ˹in the world˺ when they were fully capable ˹but they chose not to˺”*, where they are called to prostrate and cannot). The closing sentence ties the sūrah together: this is the day they were warned about, the same one a challenger mocked in the opening verses when he demanded that the punishment be brought at once (70:1 — *“A challenger has demanded a punishment bound to come”*). The answer to that demand is the picture the sūrah ends on.

**The End of the Sūrah**

The last words of the sūrah are these: eyes down and disgrace settled on them, and this is the day they were promised. The Book describes the criminals the same way elsewhere, with their heads bowed before their Lord, saying they have now seen and heard (32:12 — *“We have now seen and heard, so send us back and we will do good.”*), and it records the day when the proud are called to prostrate and cannot (68:42-43 — *“with eyes downcast, totally covered with disgrace. For they were ˹always˺ called to prostrate ˹in the world˺ when they were fully capable ˹but they chose not to˺”*). The sūrah's opening gave the reader a scoffer asking for the punishment to be brought on at once (70:1 — *“A challenger has demanded a punishment bound to come”*), and it then walked through the Day itself, the qualities of those who will be safe, and the mockers pressing in from both sides. It closes on the two words that answer all of it: the lowering of the eyes and the covering of shame. The book of the man who asked is not closed gently.
